en: Preface to the *Continued Lamp:
The Orthodox Lineage* It is heard that the splendors of Putuo are inexhaustible. Although it is said to be only several hundred li from Siming, the vast ocean lies before it;
looking west toward foreign lands, the mountains of the Three Han appear as if in the depths of the mist; to the north, it adjoins Penglai.
To its east lie Goryeo and Japan, vast and misty amidst clouds and mists.

When the ocean waves are at their most majestic, surging toward the sky and crashing against the shore, the wind and water clash so violently that one cannot distinguish even a few feet. Yet, in an instant, strange fish and dragons emerge by the hundreds.
Then, when the heavens open and the night begins, one ascends the high summit; looking out as the sun first rises over the shimmering, immense waters, the vast expanse is a boundless blur.
The sea and the sky turned entirely crimson. After a while, it leaped forth into the heavens; its final radiance shot across the waters as if swallowing and spitting them out for a long time.
I have long harbored doubts regarding what I had heard and was eager to go and witness this marvel myself.

I believe that where famous mountains and great seas manifest such spiritual wonders, there must surely be extraordinary men dwelling in deep seclusion and scholars of learning emerging from among them, coming and going.
The petitioner led along a mere merchant and a commoner; there was no scholar with whom he could converse.

He then sought among those outside the conventional world—monks dwelling in Chan hermitages—but such individuals were utterly unobtainable. My doubts increased further. Master Chan Shi Bie’an was originally a man of Shu and a dharma heir of Gao Feng.
Having come from Shu to Zhejiang, he paid homage at Mount Jing and visited Mount Tiantong, eventually taking up residence at Puzhao.
This year, Dao came to see me in Wulin and presented his work, *The Continued Lamp: The Orthodox Lineage* (*Xùdēng zhèngtǒng*), requesting that I write a preface for it.
I observed how he analyzed the genealogical lineages; by merging the Southern and Northern schools and unifying the various branches and sects, he has effectively combined the Five Lamps into one.
Could this not be what is called the "Inexhaustible Lamp" (akṣayapradīpa) in the Dharma of Vimalakīrti?

Although the fire is transmitted when the fuel is exhausted, there must necessarily have been an original piece of fuel. Now, tracing back from Master Byeol (Bie) to Dahui, we find seventeen generations.
From Dahui up to Bodhidharma, how many generations would that be? From Bodhidharma upwards to Śākyamuni, it constitutes twenty [generations].
Regarding the Eight Patriarchs: before Śākyamuni was born, one kalpa ago, there must have been one Buddha; after passing through seven more kalpas, seven Buddhas were obtained.
How many lifetimes would that correspond to? Master Bie is profound, reclusive, and fond of learning; he will surely be able to describe this for me.
I have also heard that Bodhidharma came from the West across the sea to Jinling and propagated his teaching in China. Now...
Master Bie then returned from China to propagate the school’s tradition abroad. Was this the height of his extraordinary brilliance?
Or was he perhaps accompanying the Great Being of Potalaka, appearing and disappearing amidst the mountains and seas, so that the world could never truly behold him?
Later, when I ascended Mount Siming and gazed toward Putuo from over three hundred li away, there was a radiant light piercing the heavens, vying with the sun for its brilliance.
As for this "Yao" (Radiance), it must be where the book is located. Thus follows the preface.
Written in the seventh month of the autumn of the Dingchou year of the Kangxi era by one who has received the degree of Jinshi (Presented Scholar).
Written by Yang Yongjian, Grand Master for Splendid Happiness (Guangludafu), Vice Minister of War (Bingbu Zuoshilang),

formerly Acting Governor-General of Guizhou concurrently overseeing the military affairs of Hubei, Chuan-dong, and other regions, Right Vice Censor-in-Chief (Youfuduoyi) of the Court of Judicial Inspection,

The ancient sages have said: "In the West there is a Great Sage who governs without governing and remains without disorder;
he transforms others through silence. Since Bodhidharma transmitted his Way to the Eastern Land, that Way has been one that does not rely on written words and stands outside the formal teachings.
The Separate Transmission clarifies the mind and reveals the nature, bringing an end to birth and liberation from death. When I first explored its gateway, I ultimately gained nothing;

furthermore, my practice did not accord with it in the slightest. Yet, whenever I encountered world-transcending masters who propagate the Way, they would simply raise their fists or point their fingers.

The staff and the shout were exchanged in rapid succession; amidst every word and every silence, it was as if one had passed through a butcher’s gate and could not restrain oneself from a great gorging.
In the spring of the Ren-shen year, I sailed upon the South Sea and ascended Putuo Mountain, where I met with Master Bie-an. We conversed together for several days.
I learned that [he] was the seventeenth-generation descendant of Da-hui; thus, he returned after being presented with the plaque.
The following year, the Master requested a preface for his compiled work, the *Xu deng zhengtong* (Orthodox Lineage of the Continued Lamp), from me.

Since I am already unable to fathom its inner depths, how could I dare to utter deceptive words before the Master? Nevertheless, upon carefully examining this compilation—which begins from the Southern Song dynasty and ultimately leads back to...
Today, I have gathered what was incomplete in the *Five Lamps* (Wǔdēng); this is called the *Continued Lamps* (Xùdēng).

By arranging them according to their lineages and clearly delineating each transmission, I have honored the flourishing prosperity of the two "Cassia Trees" (the Linji and Caodong schools); this is called the "Orthodox Lineage" (Zhèngtǒng).

With the lamps continued and the lineage made orthodox, one will see that lamp after lamp shall not be extinguished, its radiance flowing for a thousand years, so as to cause every person to clarify the mind and perceive the Buddha-nature.

This is the nature [of things]. To understand this is to transcend birth and death. Is it not here? Is it not here? That which is called "governing without governing and thus avoiding disorder," and "transforming through non-speaking and thus achieving self-transformation"—does it not reside in this very principle?
Does it not reside in this very principle?
In the second month of spring in the year of Kǎngxī Guīyǒu, respectfully composed by his compassionate younger brother in the Dharma, Jiāng Chényīng.

The Elder Gautama received the prediction of enlightenment from Dīpaṃkara and became the progenitor of the lamp of dhyāna.
Thereafter, it was transmitted from patriarch to patriarch, with the lamps succeeding one another so that the lineage remained undisturbed.

Although among them were those who entered the marketplace with outstretched hands, those who dwelt alone on solitary peaks, those who excelled in the power of transformation, and those who upheld the singular command of the True Dharma, their karmic conditions for retribution...
It is the same; their orthodox lineage is one and the same.

Yet, there are those whose teachings flourish in the southeast but not in the northwest, and those whose teachings flourish in the northwest but not in the southeast. All of this is rooted in the conditions of karmic retribution.
They all emerge from the same orthodox tradition. Below Mount Jing, there were the various venerable masters such as Juyun, Qingzhong, and Gaofeng. They...
Having subsequently revitalized the Linji lineage in Western Sichuan, Master Bie’an succeeded Old Man Gaofeng.
He traveled from the West to Jiangzhe, where he swept the ancestral tombs at Mount Jing and occupied the master’s seat at Putuo.
Amidst his work of forging lions and elephants, he resolved to commemorate his ancestral lineage; thus, the Ji school first [traces back] from the sixteenth generation after Caoxi to Mount Jing.
The *Shan* (Mountain) edition begins from the thirty-first generation after Caoxi and ends with the thirty-first generation.
Next, the *Huqiu* (Tiger Hill) edition begins from the sixteenth generation after Caoxi and ends with the thirty-fifth generation.

Furthermore, the *Dong* (Cave) school edition begins from Xuedou in the sixteenth generation after Caoxi and ends with the thirty-seventh generation. Additionally, it includes those whose dharma heirs are unknown and provides supplementary entries.
In all, it consists of forty-two fascicles and is titled *The Orthodox Lineage of the Continued Lamp* (*Xùdēng zhèngtǒng*). His mind was upright, his insight far-reaching, and his talent complete;
he truly may stand alongside the *Transmission of the Lamp*, the *Anthology of the Source* (*Huìyuán*), and other records to circulate throughout the world for future generations.
Those who read this compilation hereafter will suddenly encounter it directly and strike upon its truth, seeing clearly the very heart and liver of the ancients. Not yet—
Such a person surely did not exist. I, together with the Upādhyāya, have the honor of belonging to the same school. At the close of my declining years, I was fortunate enough to encounter this book;
my joy was beyond measure, and thus I have composed this preface for it.
In the fifth month of the summer during the Ren-shen year of the Kangxi era,
written by the fellow-student Fa, a Former Magistrate of Xinning and Lancheng Counties and currently a Meritorious Official (Fengzhidafu) serving as Magistrate of Shangzhou.

That the Buddhist tradition possesses the *Denglu* (Records of the Lamp) is analogous to the Confucian tradition possessing the *Tongjian* (Comprehensive Mirror). From Yao, Shun, Yu, and Tang...
The civil and martial [virtues] of the successive sovereigns throughout the ages, including their policies for governing the state and managing the people, are all recorded within the *Tongjian*.

From the patriarchs of the Śākya lineage in the East and West, down to the Chan masters of successive generations and the karmic conditions of their realization of the mind and awakening to the Way, are all recorded within the *Denglu*.

Yet, as for "refining the one and adhering to the Mean" (*jingyi zhizhong*) and "establishing the center and perfecting the ultimate" (*jianzhong jianji*), these were the principles of the emperors and kings.
This is what has been handed down through tradition. In governing the state and managing the people, how could this ever not be rooted in the mind?

Before emerging from the mother’s womb, his work of saving others was already complete—this is what the sutras and treatises praise. This clarifies that awakening to the Way through the mind is always beneficial for one's life.
Master Bie’an succeeded to Gaofeng; he is the seventeenth-generation descendant of Dahui.
In the Bingyin year, he traveled from West Shu to Jiangzhe. He swept the ancestral pagoda at Mount Jing and deposited his staff and alms bowl at Tiantong.
I, along with Provincial Commissioner Chen Gong and the various scholars of the entire prefecture, jointly requested him to take charge of the Zhenhai Chan Temple on Putuo Mountain.
His dharma influence flourished greatly, his reputation for the Way spread far and wide, and the famous mountain was thereby rendered even more renowned. Ren Shen.
In the autumn, [the compiler] presented his compilation, the *Zhengtong xu deng* (Continued Lamp of the Orthodox Tradition), and requested a preface from me.

The title "Orthodox Tradition" (*zhengtong*) makes it clear that his compilation was not undertaken casually. After I had read through it several times, I finally came to recognize the various Chan masters from Mount Jing and Tiger Hill.
Thus clarifying the mind, thus awakening to the Way, and thus engaging with others to benefit sentient beings—

how does this differ from our Confucian practice of extending knowledge, sincerity of intention, rectification of the mind, cultivation of the person, regulation of the family, governance of the state, and bringing peace to all under heaven? Indeed, that you, Reverend,

having already opened the Dharma during your wondrous life, now possess the leisure to compile the *Xu deng lu* (Continued Lamp Record) to extol the orthodox lineage— you are surely one who has returned for a second birth.
Indeed. Nevertheless, Master Zhongfeng said: "Before the Buddhas and Patriarchs were born, this lamp was already transmitted.
How about that? I request the Venerable Master to provide a turning word. [Dated] Year.

Preface:
The World-Honored One preached the Dharma for forty-nine years; it was only at the end that he was fully seen through by Kāśyapa.

Bodhidharma traveled over one hundred thousand li from the West, yet in the end, he had his marrow attained by Shen Guang. After three transmissions, the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) appeared. Six...
The *Platform Sūtra* was transmitted and practiced, all for the purpose of elucidating the profound subtleties of the Tripiṭaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
People manifest the Dharma, and the Dharma is transmitted through people. Although it is said that "no reliance is placed on words and letters," how could it ever have been apart from them?

Subsequently, the two lineages of Gui spread their fragrance, and the Five Lamps continued their flame; they wielded both "killing" and "giving life" with equal mastery, and let [their teachings] run free.

Seizing and releasing are employed together; there is the provisional and the real. Releasing and gathering both occur simultaneously; guest and host are established in tandem. The wielding of the staff and the shouting of "Ho!
are what is called being thorough and direct, solemn and dignified, lofty and ancient, meticulous and detailed, concise and clear.

When manifested as instruction, there are the formal sermons (*shàngtáng*) and the informal discourses (*xiǎocān*); when taking form through refinement, there are the general addresses (*shìzhòng*) and the universal expositions (*pǔshuō*). These are seen in various writings.
In his commentaries, he composed verses, eulogies, and independent appraisals that fully exhaust the essential meanings. He clarified what was obscure and elucidated what was profound;
even a half-phrase or a single word possessed great pivotal significance. Thus, his works accumulated into vast and extensive volumes.

The volumes were so numerous that they caused oxen to sweat as they were transported and filled the rafters of the buildings; how magnificent this was! Yet, as historical fortunes succeeded one another, periods of prosperity and decline were not constant.

Throughout the four to five hundred years spanning the end of the Song, the Yuan, and the Ming dynasties, there were times when the era was fraught with calamity, and times when the land was divided by the barrier between north and south.
Those who practice the Way are confined within remote districts and small towns; the words for governing the world have vanished amidst the wild smoke and overgrown weeds.
Humanity is nearly lost, and the Dharma has likewise declined. Yet, fortunately, the Way does not end in total extinction, for there is a principle of restoration.
Along the mountains and by the waters, there still remain one or two individuals; like a single thread binding the Nine Cauldrons, they bear the weight of the responsibility.
The thousand-jun weight of the ancestral style relied upon this to avoid falling into ruin.
Extending to the Longqing and Wanli periods of the late Ming dynasty, there was Longchi, the eighteenth-generation successor at Huqiu, who received the Dharma from Shanguo;
at that time, the orthodox lineage was still as precarious as a single strand of silk. Later, he obtained Tiantong and Qingshan, where his Way flourished greatly. Eighteen generations later...
There was Nanming, who received the Dharma from Chexi; at that time, the orthodox lineage was as fragile as a single strand of silk.
Later, he obtained Yuanhu, and his Way flourished greatly, like the nineteenth generation of Xuedou. There was Lingshan, who received the Dharma from Zongjing;
at that time, the orthodox lineage was also as fragile as a single strand of silk. Later, he obtained Shouchang, and his Way flourished greatly.
Furthermore, twenty generations later, there was a Great Awakened One who attained the Dharma at Shaoshi. At that time, the orthodox lineage was as precarious as a single strand of silk.
Later, Yunmen attained it, and his Way flourished greatly. Thirteen generations after Daoyi [Dahui], there was Chaoyang, who attained the Dharma at Qinling.
At that time, the orthodox lineage was likewise as precarious as a single strand of silk. Later, Ju Yun attained it.
His Way flourished greatly. At that time, monastic communities were arrayed like stars and spread out like clouds, mutually stimulating and uplifting one another.
Not only did the practitioners in their patched robes exclusively pursue the ultimate, but even court officials and eminent scholars came to seek the Way and examine the mind;
how much more so when...
In this illustrious era, the Great Founder, Emperor Shizu Zhang, dispatched envoys with imperial edicts everywhere, honoring and exalting the Dharma-gate.

Now, His Sacred Majesty, on his tour of inspection through the capital cities, has grandly bestowed recognition upon famous monasteries; he granted the plaque "Yunlin" (Cloud Forest) to Lingyin Monastery and inquired after its affairs.
He visited Jia Shan regarding the "Cypress Tree" koan; he stayed for two nights at Xuanmu; he traveled again to Huqiu; he ascended the pagoda of Baoen;
he walked upon the altar of Zhaoging; and he was granted a treasury grant.
The imperial edict established the Buddhist temple of Mount Jinshan Putuo.

The śramaṇa Huagong was summoned for an audience, during which the Emperor inquired about the profound meaning of the Dharma and the Way of Single Transmission; thus, this path became even more prominent at that time. Those who shoulder this Way...
There was never a time when he did not take up the guidance of later scholars; it was his self-appointed task to open the way for both humans and devas.
He produced extensive writings that accumulated into a vast number of scrolls, far exceeding the proverbial "sweat of oxen" or the "filling of rafters.

However, the records of our predecessors consist mostly of single editions, or are found among funerary inscriptions, biographies, and fragments of broken steles and manuscripts—preserving but one in ten thousand.
Throughout the various regions, it has become an urgent task for each to propagate their own school;

some have been overly selective and thus missed the essential, while others have been too eclectic and thus fallen into superficiality. Consequently, I have not declined my humble ignorance to compile this collection.
I hope that those who come after will find it beneficial upon reading it. Observe, for instance, the cases of Dahui of the Southern Song, as well as Huqiu and Ding’an.
The various patriarchs greatly revitalized the Linji and Caodong schools; their disciples and descendants multiplied what was transmitted by one into a hundred.

Nearly all were summoned by imperial decree to preach the Dharma and received the mandate to open the hall for formal sermons. They were granted titles while alive and posthumous eulogies upon death, as the emperors held the Dharma in high esteem.
How magnificent it was! Yet, when prosperity reaches its peak, decline follows.

Its corruption reached such a point that people traded in the origins of the lineage, peddled empty reputations, and relied on power and influence to claim the lineages of Yang and Zheng. Such was the inevitability of the situation; yet, in truth, it was brought about by men themselves.
Reaching down to the end of the Ming dynasty, those who rode upon the vow to support the precarious were such as Longchi, Nanming, Dajue, Lingshan, and Chaoyang.

The various masters emerged and traveled in all directions to seek out teachers; later, they retreated to dwell among forests and springs, refusing to engage in self-promotion or strive for high renown.
For several decades, they did not readily grant audiences to others; those whom they did receive were for the most part men of "copper heads and iron brows."
They were able to revitalize the reputation of their lineage. Masters such as Tiantong, Qingshan, Yuanhu, Yunmen, Shouchang, and Juyun, though separated by a thousand *li*, were truly of one mind.

At famous mountains and great monasteries, banners were raised side by side; from a state of extreme decline, they reached a time of flourishing—this was indeed natural for the times, yet it was also brought about by human effort.

General Rules.

The *Chuan deng lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp) began with Chan Master Daoyuan of the Jingde era during the Song dynasty. It was followed by the layman Li Zunxu, who compiled the *Guang deng lu* (Expanded Records of the Lamp);

Chan Master Baizhang of Foguo Temple completed the *Xu deng lu* (Continued Records of the Lamp); and Chan Master Ming of Huisheng Temple composed the *Lian deng hui yao* (Essential Collection of the Linked Lamps).
Master Leian Shouchan compiled the *Pudeng* (Universal Lamp). The *Wudeng* (Five Lamps) were widely circulated; their investigations were detailed and their language was extensive.
Master Dachuang Ji then edited them into the *Wudeng Huiyuan* (Essentials of the Five Lamps), spanning from the time of Kāśyapa Muni down to the eighteenth generation after Dajian Huineng.
His research was precise and his arguments definitive, leaving no room for further dispute. Alas, since the mid-Ming dynasty, the Dharma...

During my lifetime, the transmission has declined and much of the oral tradition has been lost. Although the *Dà bà'ēn* (Great Act of Gratitude) contains an edition of the *Xù chuán dēng lù* (Continued Record of the Transmission of the Lamp), and Master Nánshí Xiù has produced a supplementary collection, these have not been widely examined by the world.
Recently, several lamp records have appeared in succession, such as the *Bǔ dēng lù* (Supplementary Lamp Record).
Some are titled *Xùlüè* (Continued Abridgment), some *Zànxù* (Succession), some *Cúngǎo* (Surviving Drafts), some *Dàtǒng* (Great Lineage), and some *Bǎojī* (Treasury Accumulation).

In their compilation and selection, each has its own preferred approach. This work, however, uniquely searches through various collections to synthesize them into a great achievement, mutually elucidating with the *Guǎngrùn Sēngbǎo Zhuàn* (Biographies of the Jewel-like Monks of Guangrun).
It is titled *Xùdēng* (Continued Lamp), retaining the original name; it is titled *Zhèngtǒng* (Orthodox Lineage) to clarify the dharma succession.

Though the various schools differ in their branches, their source is one. By recording the eras and providing a general overview of the Great Mirror, the gradual proliferation of the lineage into a thousand or ten thousand separate sects can be forever prevented.
From the sixteenth generation of Dajian to the eighteenth, these have already been recorded in the *Huìyuán*.

Here, we begin again from the sixteenth generation because all the descendants below [Dōgen] emerged from Dahui and Huqiu, just as those above [the sixth generation] descended from Nanyue and Qingyuan.
This serves both to manifest their origins and to supplement what was incomplete in the *Huìyuán*.
Dahui and Huitong both emerged from the Linji lineage and subsequently branched out into separate lines.

This is based on the *Candeng Shipei* (Genealogy of the Lamp of Chan) by Chan Master Hongjue of Pingyang; furthermore, the succession of these two masters varied in its duration and could not be confined to a single generation.
As for their respective positions within the ancestral order (*shaomu*), I have followed the *Huiyuan Shipei* (Genealogy of the Yuan Era) without daring to introduce any personal bias.
Each lineage has its own legitimate successor; only the direct descendants may serve their ancestral patriarchs, and no one else may falsely claim them.

This is evident in the lineage records of Tiger Hill (Hǔqū), where the errors regarding Hǎizhōu Púcí and Yǒngcí have already been rectified in the *Cúngǎo*, *Bǎojí*, and various collections of the Sangha Jewels; here, we follow that established precedent.

The Cao-Dong lineage descends from Danxia through five generations. The *Da-tong* (Great Compendium) has been edited and extracted [from the records]. It identifies Lukmen Jue as being identical to Jingyin Jue, who directly inherited the lineage from Furong Kai.

The words and phrases of the ancestral masters are preserved by Fayan; even a single word or half-phrase can continue the true lineage.

Regarding their formal sermons, informal discourses, verses, and spontaneous utterances, I have collected them from the various existing anthologies. I have recorded these without composing anything new.
While the composition of works is certainly intended for the circulation of the essential insights of our school, the preservation of the human element is paramount. Thus,

even those who have not yet mastered the phrasing of these texts are included in this catalog, so that future scholars with the aspiration to collect and preserve them may utilize these titles to further augment the collection.
